claim: Approximately 6.6% of the global population carries a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).
source: Approximately 6.6% of the global population carries a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) (Kaiser et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kaiser et al., 2018

claim: Patients with T2DM are at greater risk for developing dementia and Alzheimer's disease.
source: Patients with T2DM are at greater risk for developing dementia and Alzheimer's disease (AD) and have been reported to exhibit inferior cognitive performance when compared to age-matched healthy controls (HCs) (Moheet et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moheet et al., 2015

claim: Patients with T2DM exhibit inferior cognitive performance when compared to age-matched healthy controls.
source: Patients with T2DM are at greater risk for developing dementia and Alzheimer's disease (AD) and have been reported to exhibit inferior cognitive performance when compared to age-matched healthy controls (HCs) (Moheet et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moheet et al., 2015

claim: Several human neuroimaging studies have linked T2DM with brain atrophy and cognition.
source: Several human neuroimaging studies have linked T2DM with brain atrophy and cognition (Moheet et al., 2015; Callisaya et al., 2019; Gold et al., 2007; Mankovsky et al., 2018; Manschot et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published studies

claim: T2DM results in a more rapid rate of cognitive decline than typically associated with natural aging.
source: recent research suggested that T2DM resulted in a more rapid rate of cognitive decline than typically associated with natural aging (Rawlings et al., 2014; Zilliox et al., 2016; Pelimanni and Jehkonen, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rawlings et al., 2014; Zilliox et al., 2016; Pelimanni and Jehkonen, 2018

claim: Few patients with T2DM undergo a comprehensive neurocognitive evaluation as part of their clinical care.
source: Despite strong preliminary evidence linking T2DM to neurological and cognitive decline, few patients with T2DM undergo a comprehensive neurocognitive evaluation as part of their clinical care (Zilliox et al., 2016; Biessels et al., 2006; Ninomiya, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zilliox et al., 2016; Biessels et al., 2006; Ninomiya, 2014

claim: T2DM diagnosis often occurs in middle age, hindering dissociation of patients' cognitive changes from normal aging.
source: This may reflect the fact that T2DM diagnosis often occurs in middle age, hindering dissociation of patients' cognitive changes from normal aging.
evidence: Based on inference from clinical observations

claim: The neurological effects of T2DM may reveal themselves many years before they can be detected by peripheral markers.
source: However, the neurological effects of T2DM may reveal themselves many years before they can be detected by peripheral markers (Callisaya et al., 2019; Zilliox et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Callisaya et al., 2019; Zilliox et al., 2016

claim: By the time T2DM is diagnosed and treated by standard measures, patients may have already sustained irreversible brain damage.
source: As such, by the time T2DM is diagnosed and treated by standard measures, patients may have already sustained irreversible brain damage.
evidence: Based on inference from the timing of neurological effects relative to peripheral markers

claim: The UK Biobank dataset included cognitive and neuroimaging data from N = 20,314 subjects, including 1012 T2DM and 19,302 healthy controls, aged between 50 and 80 years.
source: The UK Biobank dataset included cognitive and neuroimaging data (N = 20,314), including 1012 T2DM and 19,302 HCs, aged between 50 and 80 years.
evidence: Direct report of dataset characteristics

claim: Duration of T2DM in the UK Biobank sample ranged from 0 to 31 years with a mean of 8.5 ± 6.1 years.
source: Duration of T2DM ranged from 0 to 31 years (mean 8.5 ± 6.1 years)
evidence: Direct report of dataset characteristics

claim: In the UK Biobank sample, 498 T2DM patients were treated with metformin alone, while 352 were unmedicated.
source: 498 were treated with metformin alone, while 352 were unmedicated.
evidence: Direct report of dataset characteristics

claim: The meta-analysis evaluated 34 cognitive studies (N = 22,231) and 60 neuroimaging studies: 30 of T2DM (N = 866) and 30 of aging (N = 1088).
source: Our meta-analysis evaluated 34 cognitive studies (N = 22,231) and 60 neuroimaging studies: 30 of T2DM (N = 866) and 30 of aging (N = 1088).
evidence: Direct report of meta-analysis sample characteristics

claim: Compared to age, sex, education, and hypertension-matched healthy controls, T2DM was associated with marked cognitive deficits, particularly in executive functioning and processing speed.
source: Compared to age, sex, education, and hypertension-matched HC, T2DM was associated with marked cognitive deficits, particularly in executive functioning and processing speed.
evidence: Based on UK Biobank data analysis results

claim: T2DM was significantly associated with gray matter atrophy, primarily within the ventral striatum, cerebellum, and putamen.
source: Likewise, we found that the diagnosis of T2DM was significantly associated with gray matter atrophy, primarily within the ventral striatum, cerebellum, and putamen
evidence: Based on UK Biobank structural MRI data analysis

claim: T2DM was associated with reorganization of brain activity, with decreased activation in the caudate and premotor cortex and increased activation in the subgenual area, orbitofrontal cortex, brainstem, and posterior cingulate cortex.
source: with reorganization of brain activity (decreased in the caudate and premotor cortex and increased in the subgenual area, orbitofrontal cortex, brainstem, and posterior cingulate cortex).
evidence: Based on UK Biobank functional MRI data analysis

claim: The structural and functional changes associated with T2DM show marked overlap with the effects correlating with age but appear earlier.
source: The structural and functional changes associated with T2DM show marked overlap with the effects correlating with age but appear earlier
evidence: Based on correlation analysis between age and T2DM effects in UK Biobank data

claim: Disease duration was linked to more severe neurodegeneration in T2DM patients.
source: with disease duration linked to more severe neurodegeneration.
evidence: Based on UK Biobank analysis of disease duration effects

claim: Metformin treatment status was not associated with improved neurocognitive outcomes in T2DM patients.
source: Metformin treatment status was not associated with improved neurocognitive outcomes.
evidence: Based on UK Biobank analysis comparing medicated vs. unmedicated T2DM patients

claim: T2DM gray matter atrophy occurred approximately 26% ± 14% faster than seen with normal aging.
source: T2DM gray matter atrophy occurred approximately 26% ± 14% faster than seen with normal aging
evidence: Based on UK Biobank analysis comparing disease duration effects to age effects

claim: The neurocognitive impact of T2DM suggests marked acceleration of normal brain aging.
source: The neurocognitive impact of T2DM suggests marked acceleration of normal brain aging.
evidence: Based on inference from the overlap between T2DM and age effects

claim: Neuroimaging-based biomarkers may provide a valuable adjunctive measure of T2DM progression and treatment efficacy based on neurological effects.
source: Clinically, neuroimaging-based biomarkers may provide a valuable adjunctive measure of T2DM progression and treatment efficacy based on neurological effects.
evidence: Based on inference from the study findings about neuroimaging sensitivity

claim: In the UK Biobank dataset, executive function showed 1.9% ± 0.1% decrease in performance per year with age in individuals without T2DM.
source: The strongest effects were observed in executive function, which showed 1.9% ± 0.1% decrease in performance per year (N = 2450, T = –17.2, p<1e–10)

claim: In the UK Biobank dataset, processing speed showed 1.5% ± 0.2% decrease in performance per year with age in individuals without T2DM.

claim: T2DM was associated with a 13.1% ± 6.9% decrease in executive function performance beyond age-related effects.

claim: T2DM was associated with a 6.7% ± 3.2% decrease in processing speed performance beyond age-related effects.

claim: T2DM was associated with a 3.7% ± 2.3% decline in numeric memory performance.

claim: T2DM effects on abstract reasoning were not statistically significant in the UK Biobank dataset.

evidence: Based on UK Biobank cognitive data analysis, shown in Figure 1B

claim: T2DM effects on reaction time were not statistically significant in the UK Biobank dataset.
source: whereas abstract reasoning (T2DM: N = 886; HC: N = 886; T = –2.4, p=0.08) and reaction time (T2DM: N = 914; HC: N = 914; T = –1.0, p=0.32) were not statistically significant.
evidence: Based on UK Biobank cognitive data analysis, shown in Figure 1B

claim: The meta-analysis confirmed that individuals with T2DM exhibited markedly lower performance in executive function compared to age- and education-matched controls (K = 18, d = –0.40, p=0.009).
source: These again included executive function (K = 18, d = –0.40, p=0.009)
evidence: Based on meta-analysis of 34 cognitive studies, shown in Figure 1C

claim: The meta-analysis confirmed that individuals with T2DM exhibited markedly lower performance in processing speed compared to age- and education-matched controls (K = 31, d = –0.34, P = 5e–8).

source: verbal fluency (K = 25, d = –0.37, p=2e–8)
evidence: Based on meta-analysis of 34 cognitive studies, shown in Figure 1C

source: visuospatial reasoning (K = 13, d = –0.32, p=4e–7)

claim: Age was associated with a 0.9% ± 0.06% decrease per year in Heschl's gyrus gray matter volume in healthy controls.

source: with the most severe atrophy observed in the ventral striatum, which showed on average a 6.2% ± 1.6% further decrease in volume, beyond age-related effects (T = –7.5, p<1e-10)

claim: T2DM patients showed a 4.9% ± 1.1% further decrease in cerebellum gray matter volume beyond age-related effects.
source: in the cerebellum with an additional 4.9% ± 1.1% decrease in volume, beyond age-related effects (T = –8.8, p<1e-10)

claim: T2DM patients showed a 4.7% ± 2.3% further decrease in putamen gray matter volume beyond age-related effects.
source: and in the putamen, which showed a 4.7% ± 2.3% further decrease, beyond age-related effects (T = –4.1, p=0.002)

source: When assessed across all brain regions, T2DM-related patterns in brain atrophy exhibited strong overlap with those associated with age (r = 0.60, p=0.0002)

source: Neurocognitive effects were more severe with increased disease duration, particularly for structural changes (T = –3.8, p=0.0002)

claim: T2DM patients treated with metformin alone did not differ with respect to cognition compared to unmedicated T2DM patients after matching for disease duration and controlling for BMI.

claim: T2DM patients treated with metformin alone did not differ with respect to brain atrophy compared to unmedicated T2DM patients after matching for disease duration and controlling for BMI.
source: Even after matching groups for disease duration and controlling for BMI, T2DM patients who were treated with metformin alone (N = 498) did not differ with respect to cognition or brain atrophy compared to T2DM patients who were unmedicated (N = 352)
evidence: Based on UK Biobank analysis comparing medicated vs. unmedicated T2DM patients, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8

claim: Metformin treatment status showed no significant impact on resting-state brain activity in T2DM patients.
source: Likewise, treatment status showed no significant impact on resting-state brain activity.

claim: All reported age and T2DM effects were seen for both males and females, and strongly correlated between them.
source: All reported age and T2DM effects were seen for both males and females, and strongly correlated between them (Figure 2—figure supplement 6, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).

source: However, age and T2DM effects were stronger in males (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 5, Figure 3—figure supplement 4)

claim: The overlap between effects associated with age and T2DM was statistically significant in males for brain activation (r = 0.51, p=0.002).

claim: All females in the UK Biobank sample were menopausal and not on hormone replacement therapy.

claim: T2DM patients show deficits in cognitive performance compared to healthy controls, even after controlling for age, sex, education, and hypertension.
source: The UK Biobank dataset confirms that T2DM patients show deficits in cognitive performance compared to HC, even after controlling for age, sex, education, and hypertension.

claim: Deficits in cognitive performance in T2DM patients were accompanied by marked brain atrophy compared to age-matched healthy controls.
source: Deficits in cognitive performance were accompanied by marked brain atrophy in the T2DM sample compared to age-matched HC.

claim: The atrophy in T2DM was most severe (6.2% gray matter loss compared to healthy controls) in the ventral striatum.
source: The atrophy was most severe (6.2% gray matter loss compared to HC) in the ventral striatum, a region critical to learning, decision-making, goal-directed behavior, and cognitive control.

claim: The ventral striatum is a region critical to learning, decision-making, goal-directed behavior, and cognitive control.
source: The atrophy was most severe (6.2% gray matter loss compared to HC) in the ventral striatum, a region critical to learning, decision-making, goal-directed behavior, and cognitive control.
evidence: Based on established neuroscience knowledge

claim: Executive functioning and processing speed were the cognitive functions most affected by T2DM.
source: These cognitive functions, collectively known as executive functioning, were (with processing speed) also those most affected by T2DM.

claim: Neurodegeneration severity for all regions increased with longer T2DM disease duration.
source: Neurodegeneration severity for all regions increased with longer disease duration.

claim: Males exhibited stronger T2DM effects than females.
source: We detected qualitatively consistent results in females and males; however, males exhibited stronger effects in relation to T2DM (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).

claim: The stronger T2DM effects in males is consistent with the well-established neuroprotective effects of female hormones such as estrogen.
source: This result is consistent with the well-established neuroprotective effects of female hormones such as estrogen (Behl, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Behl, 2002

claim: The T2DM neurological effects observed result from chronic degenerative processes, which, for female participants, may have been at least partially ameliorated prior to menopause.
source: This result also suggests that the T2DM neurological effects observed result from chronic degenerative processes, which, for our female participants, may have been at least partially ameliorated prior to menopause.
evidence: Based on inference from sex differences and menopausal status

claim: Structural brain imaging can provide a clinically valuable metric for identifying and monitoring neurocognitive effects associated with T2DM.
source: Our findings indicate that structural brain imaging, in particular, can provide a clinically valuable metric for identifying and monitoring neurocognitive effects associated with T2DM.
evidence: Based on inference from the study findings about structural MRI sensitivity

claim: Structural atrophy showed global effects that were far more statistically robust (p<2e–10) than either global cognitive measures (p=0.0001) or global brain activation (p=0.002).
source: Normalizing across sample sizes to compare the measures of neurocognitive effects – structural MRI, functional MRI, and cognitive testing – structural atrophy showed global effects that were far more statistically robust (p<2e–10) than either global cognitive measures (p=0.0001) or global brain activation (p=0.002).
evidence: Based on comparison of statistical significance across modalities in UK Biobank data

claim: Structural MRI avoids confounding associated with education and practice effects compared to cognitive testing.
source: One additional advantage of structural MRI over cognitive testing is that the former avoids confounding associated with education and practice effects, and therefore may be more interpretable in real-world clinical settings in which matching for education and practice effects is not feasible.
evidence: Based on inference about methodological advantages

claim: The reorganization of brain activity seen with T2DM may reflect the brain's switch to less metabolically expensive networks to conserve energy in the face of diminishing access to glucose.
source: The reorganization of brain activity seen with T2DM may reflect the brain's switch to less metabolically expensive networks to conserve energy in the face of diminishing access to glucose, a pattern previously documented in aging (Tomasi et al., 2013; Weistuch et al., 2021; Tomasi and Volkow, 2012; Mujica-Parodi et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on inference supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The localization of brain atrophy in T2DM to the ventral striatum, followed by the cerebellum, may reflect the fact that these two brain regions contain the densest concentrations of insulin-dependent GLUT-4 compared to non-insulin-dependent isoforms GLUT-1 and GLUT-3.
source: The localization of brain atrophy in T2DM to the ventral striatum, followed by the cerebellum, may reflect the fact that these two brain regions contain the densest concentrations of insulin-dependent GLUT-4 (El Messari et al., 2002; Kobayashi et al., 1996; El Messari et al., 1998; Vannucci et al., 1998) compared to non-insulin-dependent isoforms GLUT-1 and GLUT-3.
evidence: Based on inference supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The ventral striatum functions as a critical hub within the reward circuit, integrating inputs from both cortical and subcortical regions.
source: The ventral striatum functions as a critical hub within the reward circuit, integrating inputs (including external stimuli) from both cortical and subcortical regions, and therefore is a key structure required for all learning.
evidence: Based on established neuroscience knowledge

claim: The ventral striatum is a key structure required for all learning.
source: The ventral striatum functions as a critical hub within the reward circuit, integrating inputs (including external stimuli) from both cortical and subcortical regions, and therefore is a key structure required for all learning.
evidence: Based on established neuroscience knowledge

claim: Rat studies have shown modulation of nitric oxide within the ventral striatum to control release of acetylcholine.
source: Rat studies have shown modulation of nitric oxide within the ventral striatum to control release of acetylcholine (Prast et al., 1995), a neurotransmitter severely reduced in dementia (Kurotani et al., 2003) and a target for its pharmaceutical treatment (Ferreira-Vieira et al., 2016; Muramatsu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Prast et al., 1995

claim: Acetylcholine is a neurotransmitter severely reduced in dementia.
source: Rat studies have shown modulation of nitric oxide within the ventral striatum to control release of acetylcholine (Prast et al., 1995), a neurotransmitter severely reduced in dementia (Kurotani et al., 2003) and a target for its pharmaceutical treatment (Ferreira-Vieira et al., 2016; Muramatsu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kurotani et al., 2003

claim: Acetylcholine is a target for pharmaceutical treatment of dementia.
source: Rat studies have shown modulation of nitric oxide within the ventral striatum to control release of acetylcholine (Prast et al., 1995), a neurotransmitter severely reduced in dementia (Kurotani et al., 2003) and a target for its pharmaceutical treatment (Ferreira-Vieira et al., 2016; Muramatsu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ferreira-Vieira et al., 2016; Muramatsu et al., 2019

claim: Release of nitric oxide is insulin dependent and reduced in T2DM.
source: Release of nitric oxide is insulin dependent and reduced in T2DM (Tessari et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tessari et al., 2010

claim: There is a potential mechanistic pathway between insulin resistance, atrophy of the ventral striatum, and widespread deficits with respect to learning.
source: Together, these suggest a potential mechanistic pathway between insulin resistance, atrophy of the ventral striatum, and widespread deficits with respect to learning.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple lines of evidence

claim: Memory deficits in T2DM may be primarily driven by failure to encode rather than failure to retrieve.
source: In this context, memory deficits may be primarily driven by failure to encode rather than failure to retrieve, which would be consistent with our results that did not identify the hippocampus to be one of the regions most affected.
evidence: Based on inference from the pattern of brain regions affected

claim: The structural and functional changes associated with T2DM appear earlier than age-related effects.
source: Importantly, the structural and functional changes associated with T2DM show marked overlap with age-related effects but appear earlier.
evidence: Based on inference from the overlap and disease duration analysis

claim: Neurocognitive changes seen in T2DM may progress via a common mechanistic trajectory as normal brain aging, but which is accelerated.
source: This, on the one hand, suggests that neurocognitive changes seen in T2DM may progress via a common mechanistic trajectory as normal brain aging, but which is accelerated.
evidence: Based on inference from the overlap between T2DM and age effects

claim: Brain aging itself may be a metabolic syndrome driven by impaired brain insulin signaling and glucose metabolism.
source: From another perspective, the overlap implies that brain aging itself may be a metabolic syndrome driven by impaired brain insulin signaling and glucose metabolism, the same processes that, outside the brain, are well-established with respect to T2DM.
evidence: Based on inference from the overlap between T2DM and age effects

claim: T2DM and its progression may accelerate pathways associated with typical brain aging.
source: Consistent with findings from earlier studies that focused on the brain and energy metabolism (Sokoloff, 1955; Clark, 1999), our results suggest that T2DM and its progression may accelerate pathways associated with typical brain aging.
evidence: Based on inference from study results supported by citations

claim: As T2DM diminishes glucose availability within the brain, this chronic loss of energy may compromise the brain's structure and function.
source: As T2DM diminishes s glucose availability within the brain, this chronic loss of energy may compromise the brain's structure and function .
evidence: Based on inference from study results

claim: By the time T2DM is formally diagnosed, neuronal insulin resistance may have already resulted in significant damage.
source: We consider the possibility that, by the time T2DM is formally diagnosed, neuronal insulin resistance may have already resulted in significant damage.
evidence: Based on inference from the timing of neurological effects

claim: The findings underscore the need for additional research into brain-based biomarkers for T2DM and treatment strategies that specifically target its neurocognitive effects.
source: As such, our findings underscore the need for additional research into brain-based biomarkers for T2DM and treatment strategies that specifically target its neurocognitive effects (Kaiser et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on inference from study findings

claim: Both age and T2DM were associated with decreased activation in the caudate and premotor cortex.
source: Normalized to whole-brain activation, both age (HC: N = 2250) and T2DM (T2DM: N = 646, HC: N = 646) were associated with decreased activation in the caudate and premotor cortex
evidence: Based on UK Biobank functional MRI data analysis, shown in Figure 3A

claim: Both age and T2DM were associated with increased brain activity in the subgenual area, orbitofrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, and brainstem.
source: and with increased brain activity in the subgenual area, orbitofrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, and brainstem (Figure 3A).
evidence: Based on UK Biobank functional MRI data analysis, shown in Figure 3A

claim: The NeuroQuery meta-analysis identified the same regions as UK Biobank (premotor cortex, caudate, posterior cingulate gyrus).
source: Our meta-analysis of 60 multimodal neuroimaging studies (30 age-specific, 30 T2DM-specific) independently identified the same regions as UK Biobank (premotor cortex, caudate, posterior cingulate gyrus)
evidence: Based on NeuroQuery meta-analysis, shown in Figure 3B

claim: The NeuroQuery meta-analysis additionally identified clusters of decreased activity in Broca area and the frontal eye fields.
source: but additionally identified clusters of decreased activity in Broca area and the frontal eye fields and increased activity in the thalamus and inferior temporal gyrus (Figure 3B).
evidence: Based on NeuroQuery meta-analysis, shown in Figure 3B

claim: The NeuroQuery meta-analysis additionally identified clusters of increased activity in the thalamus and inferior temporal gyrus.
source: but additionally identified clusters of decreased activity in Broca area and the frontal eye fields and increased activity in the thalamus and inferior temporal gyrus (Figure 3B).
evidence: Based on NeuroQuery meta-analysis, shown in Figure 3B

claim: The ventral striatum and cerebellum contain the densest concentrations of insulin-dependent GLUT-4.
source: The localization of brain atrophy in T2DM to the ventral striatum, followed by the cerebellum, may reflect the fact that these two brain regions contain the densest concentrations of insulin-dependent GLUT-4 (El Messari et al., 2002; Kobayashi et al., 1996; El Messari et al., 1998; Vannucci et al., 1998) compared to non-insulin-dependent isoforms GLUT-1 and GLUT-3.
evidence: Supported by citations to El Messari et al., 2002; Kobayashi et al., 1996; El Messari et al., 1998; Vannucci et al., 1998

claim: T2DM status was assessed based on self-reported diagnosis by doctor in the UK Biobank dataset.
source: T2DM status was assessed based on self-reported diagnosis by doctor.
evidence: Direct report of methodology

claim: Education was considered as a binary variable based on possession of a college degree in the UK Biobank analysis.
source: We considered education as a binary variable based on possession of a college degree.
evidence: Direct report of methodology

claim: Hypertension was quantified using measured blood pressure values: all individuals with systolic blood pressure >140 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure >90 mmHg were labeled with hypertension.
source: Hypertension was quantified using measured blood pressure values: all individuals with systolic blood pressure >140 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure >90 mmHg were labeled with hypertension (Chobanian et al., 2003).
evidence: Direct report of methodology supported by citation to Chobanian et al., 2003

claim: Female subjects who did not report menopause or if they reported ongoing hormone therapy were excluded from the UK Biobank analysis.
source: To exclude potential confounding effects due to menopausal transition, particularly relevant to the youngest age group in our sample (age cutoff >50 years), we excluded all female subjects who did not report menopause or if they reported ongoing hormone therapy (Maki and Henderson, 2016).
evidence: Direct report of methodology supported by citation to Maki and Henderson, 2016

claim: Only diabetic individuals with a self-reported age of onset ≥ 40 years were included to minimize the number of individuals with type 1 diabetes in the sample.
source: To minimize the number of individuals with type 1 diabetes in our sample, rather than type 2 diabetes, we only included diabetic individuals with a self-reported age of onset ≥ 40 years (Thomas et al., 2018).
evidence: Direct report of methodology supported by citation to Thomas et al., 2018

claim: Linear regression models were fitted to neurocognitive variables and effects were quantified as the maximum likelihood point estimates and confidence intervals (95% CIs) of the corresponding regression coefficients.
source: We fitted linear regression models to neurocognitive variables and quantified associated effects as the maximum likelihood point estimates and confidence intervals (95% CIs) of the corresponding regression coefficients.
evidence: Direct report of methodology

claim: Bonferroni correction was applied to cognitive and structural results to account for multiple comparisons.
source: To account for multiple comparisons, we applied Bonferroni correction to cognitive and structural results, and adjusted for false discovery rate (FDR) in our brain activation results
evidence: Direct report of methodology

claim: False discovery rate (FDR) adjustment was applied to brain activation results to account for multiple comparisons.
source: To account for multiple comparisons, we applied Bonferroni correction to cognitive and structural results, and adjusted for false discovery rate (FDR) in our brain activation results
evidence: Direct report of methodology

claim: Data on five cognitive domains for 18,829 participants (T2DM: N = 914, HC: N = 17,915) were extracted from the UK Biobank dataset.
source: Data on five cognitive domains for 18,829 participants (T2DM: N = 914, HC: N = 17,915) were extracted from the UK Biobank dataset, including abstract reasoning, executive function, processing speed, reaction time, and numeric memory (~2–3 s).
evidence: Direct report of dataset characteristics

claim: The five cognitive domains extracted from UK Biobank included abstract reasoning, executive function, processing speed, reaction time, and numeric memory.
source: Data on five cognitive domains for 18,829 participants (T2DM: N = 914, HC: N = 17,915) were extracted from the UK Biobank dataset, including abstract reasoning, executive function, processing speed, reaction time, and numeric memory (~2–3 s).
evidence: Direct report of dataset characteristics

claim: Gray matter volume was calculated as mm3 for the whole brain as well as for 139 anatomical regions in the UK Biobank structural MRI analysis.
source: Using structural MRI data from the UK Biobank dataset, we assessed the effects associated with T2DM (T2DM: N = 821, HC: N = 821, Appendix 1—figure 1A) compared to non-T2DM-specific age-related effects (N = 4775, Appendix 1—figure 2A) on atrophy of gray matter volume , calculated as mm3 (Callisaya et al., 2019) for the whole brain as well as for 139 anatomical regions.
evidence: Direct report of methodology supported by citation to Callisaya et al., 2019

claim: The default unilateral parcellation of 139 regions provided by UK Biobank was coarse-grained into 45 bilateral regions for region-specific analyses.
source: For region-specific analyses, we coarse-grained the default unilateral parcellation of 139 regions provided by UK Biobank into 45 bilateral regions and normalized gray matter volumes for head size.
evidence: Direct report of methodology

claim: Gray matter volumes were normalized for head size in the UK Biobank structural MRI analysis.
source: For region-specific analyses, we coarse-grained the default unilateral parcellation of 139 regions provided by UK Biobank into 45 bilateral regions and normalized gray matter volumes for head size.
evidence: Direct report of methodology

claim: Functional MRI data from UK Biobank were accessed already preprocessed according to their standard pipelines.
source: Data were accessed already preprocessed by UK Biobank according to their standard pipelines (Alfaro-Almagro et al., 2018).
evidence: Direct report of methodology supported by citation to Alfaro-Almagro et al., 2018

claim: Spatial smoothing with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 5 mm was performed on functional images after transforming to MNI space.
source: After transforming functional images to Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space, we performed spatial smoothing with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 5 mm
evidence: Direct report of methodology

claim: Brain activation was quantified by calculating the amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (ALFF) in the UK Biobank functional MRI analysis.
source: then quantified brain activation by calculating the amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (ALFF) (Zang et al., 2007).
evidence: Direct report of methodology supported by citation to Zang et al., 2007

claim: ALFF was computed from the 0.01–0.08 Hz frequency band, within a gray matter-only brain mask.
source: ALFF was computed from the 0.01–0.08 Hz frequency band, within a gray matter-only brain mask.
evidence: Direct report of methodology

claim: A significance threshold of p<0.05 and a minimum cluster size of 12 voxels (~100 mm3) was used for functional MRI statistical analyses.
source: We used a significance threshold of p<0.05 and a minimum cluster size of 12 voxels (~100 mm3) and controlled for multiple comparisons using FDR.
evidence: Direct report of methodology

claim: Time since T2DM diagnosis was derived from self-reported age at T2DM diagnosis.
source: Time since diagnosis was derived from self-reported age at T2DM diagnosis.
evidence: Direct report of methodology

claim: The reported age of onset values from three visits, separated by multiple years, were averaged to improve the accuracy of self-reported values.
source: To improve the accuracy of self-reported values, we averaged the reported age of onset values from three visits, separated by multiple years.
evidence: Direct report of methodology

claim: Fieller's theorem was used to quantify the confidence interval (95%) for the ratio of regression coefficients corresponding to T2DM duration and age.
source: To estimate the degree to which T2DM progression was associated with gray matter loss relative to age, we calculated the ratio of regression coefficients corresponding to T2DM duration and age, and expressed it as a percentage, using Fieller's theorem (Fieller, 1954) to quantify the confidence interval (95%) for this ratio.
evidence: Direct report of methodology supported by citation to Fieller, 1954

claim: For metformin treatment analysis, subjects who reported not taking any medications to treat T2DM were compared to subjects who reported taking metformin but no other medications.
source: To isolate medication effects specific to metformin, we compared subjects who reported not taking any medications to treat T2DM to subjects who reported taking metformin but no other medications.
evidence: Direct report of methodology

claim: For metformin treatment analysis, subjects were exact-matched for sex, education, and hypertension, and coarse-matched for age (bin size of 5 years) and disease duration (bin size of 3 years).
source: For these comparisons, we exact-matched for sex, education, and hypertension, and coarse-matched for age (bin size of 5 years) and disease duration (bin size of 3 years).
evidence: Direct report of methodology

claim: Body mass index (BMI) was included as a regressor in the metformin treatment analysis as a proxy measure for disease severity.
source: Since UK Biobank did not measure HbA1c levels, we also included body mass index (BMI) as a regressor since it was the only available proxy measure for disease severity (Bower et al., 2017; Bae et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct report of methodology supported by citations to Bower et al., 2017; Bae et al., 2016

claim: The cognitive meta-analysis adhered to PRISMA guidelines.
source: Our cognitive meta-analysis adhered to PRISMA guidelines (Page et al., 2021).
evidence: Direct report of methodology supported by citation to Page et al., 2021

claim: The literature search for cognitive studies yielded 219 articles.
source: Our literature search yielded 219 articles; relevant reviews were also screened for eligible studies.
evidence: Direct report of search results

claim: Seventy-five articles were identified for full-text evaluation in the cognitive meta-analysis.
source: Seventy-five articles were identified for full-text evaluation; 34 studies were eligible for inclusion.
evidence: Direct report of search results

claim: Thirty-four studies were eligible for inclusion in the cognitive meta-analysis.
source: Seventy-five articles were identified for full-text evaluation; 34 studies were eligible for inclusion.
evidence: Direct report of search results

claim: Eligible studies for the cognitive meta-analysis included a total of 4735 subjects diagnosed with T2DM and 17,496 healthy controls.
source: Eligible studies included a total of 4735 subjects diagnosed with T2DM and 17,496 HC (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Direct report of meta-analysis sample characteristics

claim: Individual cognitive tests were sorted into several domains, including abstract reasoning, executive function, processing speed, numeric memory, visual memory, verbal memory, verbal fluency, visuospatial reasoning, and working memory.
source: We sorted individual cognitive tests into several domains, including abstract reasoning, executive function, processing speed, numeric memory, visual memory, verbal memory, verbal fluency, visuospatial reasoning, and working memory (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Direct report of methodology

claim: Cognitive differences between participants diagnosed with T2DM and healthy controls were determined by calculating standardized mean difference (SMD) effect sizes and 95% CIs for all cognitive domains.
source: Cognitive differences between participants diagnosed with T2DM and HC were determined by calculating standardized mean difference (SMD) effect sizes and 95% CIs for all cognitive domains.
evidence: Direct report of methodology

claim: Effect sizes were calculated as Cohen's d by dividing the mean difference in group scores by the pooled standard deviation of individual domains.
source: We calculated effect sizes as Cohen's d by dividing the mean difference in group scores by the pooled standard deviation of individual domains (Cohen, 1988)
evidence: Direct report of methodology supported by citation to Cohen, 1988

claim: Random-effects models were used to account for variability between samples not due to sampling error with significance at p<0.05.
source: We used random-effects models to account for variability between samples not due to sampling error with significance at p<0.05, and effect size heterogeneity was evaluated using values for Cochran's Q and I (Moheet et al., 2015; Higgins et al., 2003).
evidence: Direct report of methodology supported by citations to Moheet et al., 2015; Higgins et al., 2003

claim: NeuroQuery is an automated Coordinate-Based Meta-Analysis tool based on a database of z-scores collected by crawling through texts and tables of published research articles by an automated algorithm.
source: NeuroQuery is an automated Coordinate-Based Meta-Analysis (Fox et al., 1998; Van Horn et al., 2004; Yarkoni et al., 2010) tool based on a database of z-scores collected by crawling through texts and tables of published research articles by an automated algorithm (Yarkoni et al., 2011).
evidence: Direct report of methodology supported by citations

claim: NeuroQuery optimizes for rigor and reproducibility by utilizing predictive modeling, a higher threshold for results than statistical significance.
source: NeuroQuery optimizes for rigor and reproducibility by utilizing predictive modeling, a higher threshold for results than statistical significance.
evidence: Direct report of methodology

claim: In a quantitative evaluation of its generalization performance with 16-fold cross-validation and 10:90 test-train splits, NeuroQuery was found to accurately produce brain maps for out-of-sample neuroimaging studies.
source: In a quantitative evaluation of its generalization performance with 16-fold cross-validation and 10:90 test-train splits, NeuroQuery was found to accurately produce brain maps for out-of-sample neuroimaging studies (Yarkoni et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yarkoni et al., 2011

claim: The NeuroQuery database in total contains 149,000 neuroimaging papers and represents the single largest database of neuroimaging foci to date.
source: The database in total contains 149,000 neuroimaging papers and represents the single largest database of neuroimaging foci to date.
evidence: Direct report of database characteristics

claim: The search terms used to obtain the meta-analytic maps from NeuroQuery were 'diabetic' and 'age'.
source: The search terms we used to obtain the meta-analytic maps were "diabetic" and "age."
evidence: Direct report of methodology

claim: The NeuroQuery search terms identified the 30 most relevant neuroimaging studies for T2DM and 30 most relevant neuroimaging studies for age.
source: These terms identified the 30 most relevant neuroimaging studies for T2DM and 30 most relevant neuroimaging studies for age (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Direct report of search results

claim: In the T2DM datasets from NeuroQuery, 23 were fMRI (ALFF), 2 were structural (T1), 3 were FDG positron emission tomography (PET), and 2 were tractography (diffusion tensor imaging [DTI]).
source: In the T2DM datasets, 23 were fMRI (ALFF), 2 were structural (T1), 3 were FDG positron emission tomography (PET), and 2 were tractography (diffusion tensor imaging [DTI]).
evidence: Direct report of dataset characteristics

claim: In the age datasets from NeuroQuery, 22 were fMRI (ALFF), 3 were structural (T1), and 5 were tractography (DTI, diffusion weighted imaging).
source: In the age datasets, 22 were fMRI (ALFF), 3 were structural (T1), and 5 were tractography (DTI, diffusion weighted imaging).
evidence: Direct report of dataset characteristics
